fields.title: What waiting looks like
fields.keyTakeaway: An intermediate state is a fully-fledged product screen: it must have a time limit, a clear outcome, and protection against double-tapping.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: There is a gap between "clicked" and "done". What does the user see during this time, and why is this product work rather than design?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Intermediate states are designed last and as an afterthought, yet the user sees them with every action. A poorly designed wait screen generates duplicates, support tickets, and the feeling that the product is broken—even when the system works perfectly.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Four ways to handle waiting, from the fastest-appearing to the most honest.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[optimistic-ui|Optimistic UI]].** We show the result immediately without waiting for the server. A like is placed instantly, an item appears in the cart right away. Works when the operation is almost always successful and rollback is painless. Doesn't work where a refusal is likely or costly: showing "paid" before confirmation is deception.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Indicator with text.** Not a spinning circle, but an explanation of what is happening. "Checking availability" is better than a spinner because it sets expectations for duration and explains the delay.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Step-by-step progress.** For long operations: "Checking stock → Creating order → Confirming payment". The user sees movement, and three seconds with movement are easier to bear than two without.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Deferred result.** The operation goes to the background, the screen is freed up, the result arrives via notification. The only option for truly long operations.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Three rules whose violation costs the most:
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *Endless waiting is unacceptable.* Any "in progress" state must have a limit and transition to a clear outcome.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *Double-tapping must not repeat the operation.* The button gets blocked, and idempotency must also work on the server because button blocking is not protection.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: *The user must be warned about a long operation in advance,* rather than after they start waiting. "Generating the report will take up to 5 minutes, we'll send a notification" before starting is entirely different from the same text appearing a minute later.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Exporting a year's purchase history: deferred result. Button → "Preparing file, we'll send a notification, usually takes 2–3 minutes" → screen is freed. The warning stands before the click, in the button description.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Adding to cart: optimistic UI. The item appears instantly, the counter increases locally. If the server denies it—the item disappears with an explanation. Refusals are rare, and immediacy matters more.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Checkout: indicator with text plus time escalation, discussed in the previous node. Optimistic UI is unacceptable here—you cannot show "order placed" before payment confirmation.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: A special find: the "Order is being placed" screen received a "Minimize" button with the promise to send a notification. 8% of users use it—those for whom the wait dragged on. Previously, these people would close the app and have no idea how it ended.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Optimistic UI requires a thoughtful rollback, and rollback almost always looks worse than honest waiting. It should be used where the probability of failure is noticeably lower than a percentage.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: An intermediate state is a fully-fledged product screen: it must have a time limit, a clear outcome, and protection against double-tapping.
